fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes a homogeneous single-phase alloy, whereas the target material is as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 with FCC and B2 phases.

It attributes embrittlement to grain-boundary elemental segregation, contrary to the target mechanism of enhanced L12 ordering, elevated APBE, planar slip, and stress concentration at jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary tips.
It replaces controlled thermal aging with simultaneous prolonged high-temperature mechanical loading, confounding exposure history with the mechanical test.
It misses the non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile response: maximum embrittlement near 600°C and recovery near 750°C.
No supporting prior evidence is cited, and the proposed temperatures and exposure durations are asserted without justification.
explanation: The response addresses toughness loss and offers a nominal control, microstructural measurements, and a falsification rule, but it reconstructs neither the material nor the governing intervention and mechanism. Its generic segregation hypothesis resembles classical grain-boundary embrittlement—the comparison mechanism that the target evidence is meant to exclude. The experiment could test segregation, but the loaded/high-temperature group versus an unloaded/room-temperature control cannot separate thermal aging from mechanical-loading effects and does not map the 550–750°C brittle window. It also fails to examine L12 ordering, APBE-related slip behavior, jagged FCC/B2 boundaries, dislocation pile-ups, or crack initiation at phase-boundary tips. The generic prediction of reduced toughness captures only one part of the behavior and omits ductility recovery at 750°C. In the absence of citations or alloy-specific evidence, this is not a well-supported alternative.
